wine.name: Château Lafite Rothschild
wine.classification: Premier Cru Classé in the 1855 classification of the Médoc
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with Merlot and small parts of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: Deep gravel slopes in the north of Pauillac, running to the border with Saint-Estèphe, and the Carruades plateau beside them.
wine.making: Fermented parcel by parcel in wooden and steel vats, then aged for about a year and a half in new oak barrels, many of them made by the estate's own coopers, before it is bottled at the château.
wine.glass: Cedar, pencil shavings and cassis over violet and graphite, more perfume than power, with fine, firm tannin, fresh acidity and a long, dry finish of cigar box.
wine.ageing: Closed for its first ten to fifteen years in a strong vintage, it can then hold and develop for half a century.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, and an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The commune appellation, red wine only, between Saint-Julien and Saint-Estèphe.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant in Bordeaux.
The family name the estate took after Baron James de Rothschild bought it in 1868.

records.table: Château Lafite Rothschild stands first in the 1855 list of the Médoc's first growths: Pauillac, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon, from gravel by the Saint-Estèphe border. Expect cedar, pencil shavings and cassis, more perfume than power, built to age for decades.
records.story: Vines were planted at Lafite in the late seventeenth century, most likely by Jacques de Ségur, and his grandson Nicolas-Alexandre de Ségur (1697 to 1755), remembered as the Prince of the Vines, made the wine known at the court of Louis XV. Debts and the Revolution broke the Ségur holding: the estate was sold at public auction in the 1790s and passed through several hands. When the Bordeaux brokers drew up their classification for the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1855, Lafite stood first among the four first growths. On 8 August 1868 Baron James de Rothschild (1792 to 1868), head of the family's Paris bank, bought it at auction against a group of Bordeaux merchants who drove the bidding up; he died three months later. The estate took the family's name and carried it through phylloxera, two world wars and the lean years between them. The Carruades plateau beside the vineyard gives its name to the second wine, Carruades de Lafite. For a sommelier, Lafite is the reference for the perfumed, restrained side of Pauillac, the first growth that whispers rather than shouts.

others.name: Carruades de Lafite
others.note: The second wine, named for the Carruades plateau, with more Merlot than the grand vin.

traps: Carruades de Lafite is the second wine, not the grand vin.
Lafite is in Pauillac, not Saint-Estèphe, though its vines run to the border.
Lafite and Mouton were bought by different branches of the Rothschild family, Mouton in 1853 and Lafite in 1868.

cards.front: Château Lafite Rothschild: who bought it in 1868, and what happened next?
cards.back: Baron James de Rothschild of the Paris bank, at auction; he died three months later and the estate took the family's name.

cards.front: Which grape leads Château Lafite Rothschild, and what is its second wine?
cards.back: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority; the second wine is Carruades de Lafite.

questions.q: A guest wants the second wine of Château Lafite Rothschild. Which bottle do you bring?
questions.exp: Carruades de Lafite, named for a plateau beside the vineyard, is Lafite's second wine; Les Forts is Latour's, Pavillon Rouge is Margaux's and Le Petit Mouton is Mouton's.

questions.q: Which first growth did Baron James de Rothschild buy at auction in August 1868, months before his death?
questions.exp: He bought Lafite on 8 August 1868 and died that November; Brane-Mouton had been bought by Nathaniel de Rothschild in 1853 and renamed Mouton.

wine.name: Château Latour
wine.classification: Premier Cru Classé in the 1855 classification of the Médoc
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, by far the larger part, with Merlot and touches of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: L'Enclos, the walled heart of the estate on deep gravel above the Gironde at the southern edge of Pauillac, by the Saint-Julien border; fruit from outside it goes to the second and third wines.
wine.making: Fermented in temperature controlled stainless steel vats, first installed in 1964, and aged for well over a year in new oak barrels before bottling at the château; the wines are then held at the estate until it judges them ready.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackberry and cigar box over graphite and an iron, almost bloody note; dense and grippy, with high, firm tannin, fresh acidity and a long, tight finish.
wine.ageing: Austere for fifteen to twenty years in a strong vintage, it then lasts for decades, and it holds its shape even in weak years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The first wine, as the label prints it, drawn from L'Enclos.
The commune appellation, red wine only, between Saint-Julien and Saint-Estèphe.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant in Bordeaux.

records.table: Château Latour is the Pauillac first growth named for the tower that guarded the Gironde in the Hundred Years War. Mostly Cabernet Sauvignon from the walled Enclos, it is dense and firm and needs decades, so decant it well.
records.story: A fortified tower stood here in the fourteenth century, guarding the estuary during the Hundred Years War, and it gave the estate its name; the round tower that stands there now, and on every label, was built later. By the early eighteenth century Latour had joined Lafite in the hands of the Ségur family, and in 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked it among the four first growths. The Ségur heirs kept it until 1963, when they sold a majority to the British Pearson group, with Harveys of Bristol beside it. The new owners rebuilt the cellar and in 1964 replaced the old wooden vats with temperature controlled stainless steel, three years after Haut-Brion and well ahead of most of Bordeaux. Les Forts de Latour, the second wine, followed with the 1966 vintage, and the estate returned to French hands in 1993. Latour is famous for consistency: its deep gravel by the river gives a wine that holds its shape in weak years, and its 1961 is a vintage of history. With the 2012 vintage it left the en primeur system, the sale of wine still in barrel, and has since released its wines when it judges them ready to drink.

others.name: Les Forts de Latour
others.note: The second wine, first released with the 1966 vintage, mostly from parcels outside L'Enclos.

others.name: Pauillac de Latour
others.note: The third wine, labelled simply by its commune.

traps: Les Forts de Latour is the second wine, not the grand vin.
Château Latour in Pauillac is a different estate from Latour-Martillac in Pessac-Léognan and La Tour Carnet in the Haut-Médoc.
Latour left the en primeur system with the 2012 vintage, so its wines reach the market only when the estate releases them.

cards.front: Château Latour: what is L'Enclos, and what wine does it give?
cards.back: The walled heart of the estate on deep gravel above the Gironde; it gives the grand vin, while other parcels go to the second and third wines.

cards.front: What did Château Latour change in its cellar in 1964?
cards.back: It replaced its wooden vats with temperature controlled stainless steel, three years after Haut-Brion.

questions.q: A guest asks why Château Latour is known for holding up even in weak vintages. Which reason fits?
opts: Deep gravel by the Gironde in the walled Enclos
A high share of Merlot on cool clay
Grapes bought from across the Haut-Médoc
Long ageing in large old casks
questions.exp: L'Enclos lies on deep, warm gravel beside the estuary, which drains well and ripens Cabernet Sauvignon even in hard years; the blend is mostly Cabernet, not Merlot.

questions.q: In 1963 a majority of Château Latour was sold to new owners who then modernised its cellar. Who were they?
opts: The British Pearson group, with Harveys of Bristol
The Paris bank of the Rothschild family
The Bordeaux merchant house of Ginestet
questions.exp: The Ségur heirs sold a majority to Pearson, with Harveys of Bristol, in 1963; the new owners put in stainless steel vats in 1964.

wine.name: Château Margaux
wine.classification: Premier Cru Classé in the 1855 classification of the Médoc
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the larger part, with Merlot and a little Petit Verdot and Cabernet Franc.
wine.sites: Gravel croupes, low rises of deep gravel, in the commune of Margaux around the château; a separate parcel of Sauvignon Blanc gives the white.
wine.making: Fermented in oak and steel vats, parcel by parcel, and aged for eighteen months to two years in new oak barrels, many made by the estate's own coopers, before bottling at the château.
wine.glass: Violet, rose petal and cassis over cedar and cool graphite, with blackberry and a little liquorice; fine grained, silky tannin, bright acidity and a long, lifted finish.
wine.ageing: Charming earlier than Latour, it still needs ten to fifteen years in a strong vintage and can last half a century.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Both the estate and the commune appellation, red only; the estate's white is sold as Bordeaux.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant in Bordeaux.

records.table: Château Margaux is the first growth of the Margaux appellation, a Cabernet Sauvignon led wine of violets, cassis and silk, made behind a neoclassical château of the 1810s. Its white, Pavillon Blanc, is sold as plain Bordeaux.
records.story: The estate was shaped in the sixteenth century by the Lestonnac family, who turned a medieval domain called La Mothe towards wine. In 1787 Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826), then the American minister in Paris, toured Bordeaux and named Château Margaux among four wines of the first quality, with Latour, Haut-Brion and Lafite. After the Revolution the Marquis de la Colonilla bought the estate in the early nineteenth century and had the architect Louis Combes build the neoclassical château, begun in 1810, that appears on the label. In 1855 the brokers ranked Château Margaux a first growth, one of only four reds. The twentieth century brought hard times: the Ginestet family, Bordeaux merchants, held it through lean decades and sold it in 1977 to André Mentzelopoulos (1915 to 1980), who restored the vineyards and cellars before his death, with the oenologist Émile Peynaud (1912 to 2004) as adviser. The run of vintages from 1978 onwards brought the estate's name back. Its white, Pavillon Blanc, is all Sauvignon Blanc, and since the Margaux appellation is for red wine alone it must be sold as Bordeaux Blanc.

others.name: Pavillon Rouge du Château Margaux
others.note: The second wine, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from the estate.

others.name: Pavillon Blanc du Château Margaux
others.note: All Sauvignon Blanc, sold as Bordeaux Blanc because the Margaux appellation is red only.

traps: Pavillon Blanc is appellation Bordeaux Blanc, never appellation Margaux.
Pavillon Rouge is the second wine; Pavillon Blanc is a different wine altogether.
A Margaux on a list is not necessarily the first growth: the appellation holds many estates.

cards.front: Château Margaux's white wine: what is it, and how is it labelled?
cards.back: Pavillon Blanc du Château Margaux, all Sauvignon Blanc, labelled Bordeaux Blanc because the Margaux appellation admits only red.

cards.front: Who bought Château Margaux in 1977, and what followed?
cards.back: André Mentzelopoulos, who restored the vineyards and cellars with Émile Peynaud's advice; the vintages from 1978 brought the estate's name back.

questions.q: A guest orders Château Margaux's white wine and asks why the label says Bordeaux rather than Margaux. What do you explain?
opts: The Margaux appellation covers red wine only
The white grows in the Entre-Deux-Mers
The white is a blend of bought grapes
The 1855 rank forbids a white Margaux
questions.exp: Pavillon Blanc grows on the estate, but the Margaux appellation, like every commune appellation of the Médoc, is for red wine, so the white is sold as Bordeaux Blanc.

questions.q: In 1787 an American diplomat touring Bordeaux named Château Margaux among four wines of the first quality. Who was he?
questions.exp: Thomas Jefferson, then minister in Paris, named Margaux, Latour, Haut-Brion and Lafite in 1787, close to the four red first growths of 1855.

wine.name: Château Haut-Brion
wine.classification: Premier Cru Classé in 1855, and a Cru Classé de Graves for its red in 1959
wine.grapes: Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon in near equal parts, with Cabernet Franc and a little Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: Two gravel hillocks in Pessac, now surrounded by the suburbs of Bordeaux, whose warmth ripens the grapes early.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel vats, which the estate installed in 1961, the first of the first growths to do so, and aged for eighteen months to two years in new oak barrels before bottling at the château.
wine.glass: Tobacco leaf, cigar box and wood smoke over cassis and ripe black cherry, with warm gravel, a little truffle and fine, sweet tannin; savoury, supple and long.
wine.ageing: Open sooner than the Pauillac first growths, it still rewards fifteen years and can last for more than half a century.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The appellation of the northern Graves, created in 1987, where Haut-Brion lies.
The older name of the district, printed on bottles from before Pessac-Léognan was carved out of it.
Bottled at the estate rather than by a merchant in Bordeaux.

records.table: Château Haut-Brion is the one first growth of 1855 outside the Médoc, from gravel hillocks in Pessac now inside the city's suburbs. Near equal Merlot and Cabernet give tobacco, wood smoke and cassis, softer and more savoury than the Pauillacs.
records.story: Jean de Pontac married into the Haut-Brion lands in 1525 and acquired the estate in 1533, and his descendants made it one of the first Bordeaux wines sold under the name of its own estate. Arnaud III de Pontac (1599 to 1681) sold it in London, and on 10 April 1663 Samuel Pepys (1633 to 1703) wrote in his diary of drinking a French wine called Ho Bryan, an early written note on a Bordeaux estate. Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826) visited in 1787 and bought its wine, and the statesman Talleyrand (1754 to 1838) owned it briefly in the early nineteenth century. In 1855 the brokers could not leave it out: it was ranked a first growth beside three Médoc estates, though it lies in the Graves. The American banker Clarence Dillon (1882 to 1979) bought it in 1935. In 1959 it was classified again, among the red Crus Classés de Graves, and in 1961 it became the first of the first growths to ferment in stainless steel vats. Its white, Haut-Brion Blanc, is one of the few dry white wines of Bordeaux to stand beside the reds.

others.name: Le Clarence de Haut-Brion
others.note: The second wine, called Bahans Haut-Brion until the 2007 vintage.

others.name: Château Haut-Brion Blanc
others.note: The dry white of Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc, made in very small quantity.

traps: Haut-Brion is in Pessac-Léognan, in the Graves, not the Médoc, despite its rank of 1855.
It is classified twice: as a first growth in 1855 and among the Graves Crus Classés in 1959.
La Mission Haut-Brion, across the road, is a separate estate.

cards.front: Château Haut-Brion: why is it the odd one out among the first growths?
cards.back: It lies in Pessac, in the Graves, the one estate of the 1855 list outside the Médoc.

cards.front: Château Haut-Brion appears in a London diary of 1663: whose, and under what name?
cards.back: Samuel Pepys, on 10 April 1663, who wrote of a French wine called Ho Bryan.

questions.q: Blind, a first growth shows tobacco, wood smoke and soft cassis from a blend of near equal Merlot and Cabernet. Which appellation fits?
questions.exp: Haut-Brion, in Pessac-Léognan, blends Merlot and Cabernet in near equal parts on warm gravel, giving smoke and tobacco; the Pauillac and Margaux first growths are Cabernet led.

questions.q: Which American bought Château Haut-Brion in 1935, beginning the estate's modern era?
questions.exp: The banker Clarence Dillon bought Haut-Brion in 1935; Jefferson had visited in 1787, and Mondavi's tie to Bordeaux was Opus One with Mouton.

wine.name: Château Mouton Rothschild
wine.classification: Premier Cru Classé since 1973; a second growth in the 1855 classification
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with Merlot and small parts of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: The Mouton plateau of deep gravel in the north of Pauillac, beside Lafite.
wine.making: Fermented in large oak vats, parcel by parcel, and aged for around twenty months in new oak barrels before bottling at the château, where the whole crop has been bottled since the 1924 vintage.
wine.glass: Cassis, blackcurrant leaf and mint over cigar box, roasted coffee and sweet cedar; opulent and dense, with firm, ripe tannin, fresh acidity and a long finish of clove and graphite.
wine.ageing: Opulent enough to tempt early, it needs fifteen years in a strong vintage and can last for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Since 1945 a different artist has made the work at the head of each year's label.
The commune appellation, red wine only, between Saint-Julien and Saint-Estèphe.
Bottled at the estate, which Mouton did with its whole crop from 1924.

records.table: Château Mouton Rothschild is the Pauillac first growth that had to fight for its rank: promoted in 1973, the one promotion in the 1855 list. Cabernet Sauvignon gives cassis, cigar box and coffee, and every vintage carries an artist's label.
records.story: Baron Nathaniel de Rothschild (1812 to 1870), of the English branch of the family, bought Château Brane-Mouton in 1853 and gave it his family's name. Two years later the brokers' classification of 1855 placed it at the head of the second growths, a slight the family never accepted. His great grandson, Baron Philippe de Rothschild (1902 to 1988), took charge in 1922 and changed Bordeaux: from the 1924 vintage he bottled the whole crop at the château, when most estates sold their wine in cask to merchants, and that year's label was drawn by the poster artist Jean Carlu (1900 to 1997). In 1945 he marked the Liberation with a label bearing a V for victory by Philippe Jullian (1919 to 1977), and since then a different artist has made part of each year's label. The old motto ran: first I cannot be, second I do not deign, Mouton I am. After decades of campaigning, a decree of 1973 made Mouton a first growth, and the motto became: first I am, second I was, Mouton does not change. In 1979 Philippe de Rothschild founded Opus One in Napa with Robert Mondavi (1913 to 2008).

others.name: Le Petit Mouton de Mouton Rothschild
others.note: The second wine, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from the estate.

others.name: Aile d'Argent
others.note: The dry white of Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, sold as Bordeaux Blanc.

traps: The 1973 promotion is the one change of rank in the 1855 red list; no estate has been demoted.
Mouton Cadet is a merchant's brand from the same family, not the estate's second wine.
Mouton was bought in 1853 by the English branch of the Rothschilds; Lafite came to the French branch in 1868.

cards.front: Château Mouton Rothschild: what changed in 1973?
cards.back: A decree promoted it from second growth to first growth, the one promotion in the 1855 list, and its motto changed to first I am, second I was, Mouton does not change.

cards.front: What has Château Mouton Rothschild's label carried each year since 1945?
cards.back: A work by a different artist, a series begun with the V for victory label marking the Liberation.

questions.q: A guest at a Bordeaux dinner wants the dry white made at Château Mouton Rothschild. Which wine is it?
questions.exp: Aile d'Argent is the estate's dry white, sold as Bordeaux Blanc; Pavillon Blanc is Margaux's, Le Petit Mouton is the second red, and Mouton Cadet is a merchant's brand.

questions.q: In which year was Château Mouton Rothschild promoted from second growth to first growth by decree?
questions.exp: A decree of 1973 made Mouton a first growth, the one promotion in the 1855 list; 1924 was its first whole château bottling and 1945 the first label of the artist series.
